title: Dinner and the rules of hospitality
goal: Order food, praise the cooking, and turn down second helpings without giving offense — inside a culture that treats a guest as a sacred duty, not an accident.
bekal: name Afghan dishes and order at a restaurant
praise the cooking and politely decline more food
understand the unwritten rules of مېلمستیا in someone's home

dialogs.title: خبرې اترې — د ماښام ډوډۍ
dialogs.intro: Thursday night, the eve of Friday. The whole family has gathered, the eating cloth is spread on the floor, and dishes arrive faster than anyone can finish them.

lines.speaker: انا:
lines.text: بودي، راځه کېنه. ډوډۍ چمتو ده.
lines.baca: Būdī, rādza kena. ḍoḍəy chamto da.
lines.id: Budi, come and sit down. The food is ready.
lines.literal: Budi, come sit. food ready is.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: ډېره مننه. دا څه دي؟ ډېر ښه بوی لري.
lines.baca: ḍera manana. dā tsə dī? ḍer ṣa boy larī.
lines.id: Thank you very much. What's this? It smells wonderful.
lines.literal: much thanks. this what is? very good smell has-it.

lines.speaker: انا:
lines.text: دا قابلي پلو دی، زمونږ ملي خواړه.
lines.baca: dā qābilī palaw day, zmūẓ millī khwāṛa.
lines.id: This is Kabuli palaw, our national dish.
lines.literal: this Kabuli palaw is, of-us national food.

lines.speaker: انا:
lines.text: وریجې، د پسه غوښه، ګازره او کشمش.
lines.baca: wrīje, də psə ghwaṣa, gāzara aw kishmish.
lines.literal: rice, of sheep meat, carrots and raisins.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: کشمش په وریجو کې؟ دا زمونږ لپاره نوی دی.
lines.baca: kishmish pə wrījo ke? dā zmūẓ ləpāra naway day.
lines.id: Raisins in rice? That's new to us.
lines.literal: raisins in rice in? this of-us for new is.

lines.speaker: انا:
lines.text: وڅکئ! خوږ او مالګین سره یو ځای خوند لري.
lines.baca: wətsakəy! khwaẓ aw mālgīn sara yaw dzāy khwand larī.
lines.id: Try it! Sweet and salty together is delicious.
lines.literal: taste-you(pl)! sweet and salty together one place taste has-it.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: ډېر خوندور دی! تاسو ښه پخوانه یاست.
lines.baca: ḍer khwandwar day! tāso ṣa pakhwāna yāst.
lines.id: It's delicious! You're a wonderful cook.
lines.literal: very tasty is! you(pl) good cook(f) are.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: بس دی، مننه. زه موړ یم.
lines.baca: bas day, manana. zə moṛ yəm.
lines.id: That's enough, thank you. I'm full.
lines.literal: enough is, thanks. I full am-I.

lines.speaker: انا:
lines.text: موړ؟ لا خو دې هېڅ نه دي خوړلي!
lines.baca: moṛ? lā kho de hets nə dī khoṛəlī!
lines.id: Full? You haven't eaten anything yet!
lines.literal: full? still but you at-all nothing eaten-have!

lines.speaker: نجیب:
lines.text: بودي، دا زمونږ دود دی. لږ نور واخله.
lines.baca: Būdī, dā zmūẓ dod day. ləẓ nor wākhla.
lines.id: Budi, this is our custom. Have a little more.
lines.literal: Budi, this of-us custom is. little more take.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: ښه، لږ نور. خو بیا رښتیا بس!
lines.baca: ṣa, ləẓ nor. kho byā riṣtyā bas!
lines.id: OK, a little more. But after that, really enough!
lines.literal: good, little more. but then really enough!

lines.speaker: انا:
lines.text: خدای دې برکت کړي. مېلمه د خدای رحمت دی.
lines.baca: khudāy de barakat kṛī. melma də khudāy rahmat day.
lines.id: May God bless you. A guest is a mercy from God.
lines.literal: God may blessing do. guest of God mercy is.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: ستاسو مېلمستیا زه هېڅکله نه هېروم.
lines.baca: stāso melmastyā zə hetskəla nə herawəm.
lines.id: I will never forget your hospitality.
lines.literal: of-you(pl) hospitality I never not forget-I.

notes: ⚠️ Saying no once is not saying no. In Afghanistan food is offered two or three times, and the host takes your first refusal as politeness, not as an answer. If you really are full, accept **a little** at the second offer — that is the way out everyone understands.
The sentence بس دی، مننه is the gentlest refusal, and it must be said while still smiling and placing your hand on your chest. Refusing with a blank face reads as not liking the food.
The word خوند means "taste" and خوندور means "tasty". Stronger praise: ډېر خوندور دی or د ګوتو خولې دي (literally "the fingers are sweet", a compliment to the cook).

Notice the word شته *shta* in the fourth line, which means "there is". It is the partner of نشته *nishta* (there isn't), which you have already seen, and neither ever changes form — two words that will never give you trouble.
The phrase خدای دې برکت کړي is the most common thing to say at the end of a meal, and the reply is simply مننه or آمین. It is used by hosts and guests alike.

The word مېلمستیا is more than "hospitality". It is one of the pillars of **پښتونولي**, the unwritten Pashtun code of life, older than any state. Treating a guest well is not a personal choice but a duty, and that is why your refusal is never accepted on the first try.

grammars.title: Two words for "there is" and "there isn't": شته and نشته
body: Pashto has separate words for existence, apart from the verb "to be". The word شته means "there is" or "is available", and نشته means "there isn't".
Neither **ever changes form**: they don't follow gender and they don't follow number. This is one of the few places where Pashto gives you a complete rest.

grammars.title: Offering, accepting, and declining
body: The sentences in the first column are what the host will say to you; the ones in the third column are what you need on the tip of your tongue. Learn both, because this conversation repeats in every home you enter.
⚠️ Notice that a refusal almost always opens with **مننه**. Declining without saying thank you sounds harsh in Pashto — much harsher than "no thanks" in English.

blocks.text: Tastes, and how to give praise

blocks.title: ⚠️ Hungry and thirsty agree in gender
items: The words وږی *wəẓay* (hungry) and تږی *təẓay* (thirsty) behave like adjectives, so both change: a man says **زه وږی یم**, a woman says **زه وږې یم**.

This differs from Persian and Urdu, which use a sentence shaped like "to me there is hunger". Pashto is closer to English here — "I am hungry" — except that the adjective agrees with whoever is speaking.
Full sentences you will use often: **زه ډېر وږی یم** (I'm very hungry) and **اوبه غواړم، تږی یم** (I'd like water, I'm thirsty).

blocks.title: The unwritten rules of an Afghan home
items: Take your shoes off at the door. The eating cloth is spread on the carpeted floor, and that floor is clean.
Sit cross-legged. **Don't** stretch out your legs with the soles of your feet toward other people or toward the food; this is considered rude throughout the region.
Eat with your **right** hand, and give and receive with your right hand. Bread is torn with the right hand and used as a scoop.
The guest is served the best pieces of meat first, and refusing them won't work. Accept, say **مننه**, and share some with the child sitting next to you — that is always welcomed.
⚠️ Don't praise any one object in someone's home too earnestly. In some areas the host will feel obliged to give it to you, and turning down that gift is much harder than holding back your praise.

items: The host says نور واخله and you are already full.
The host says چای وڅښه and you'd like some.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: دا څه دی؟ — ډېر خوندور دی! — بس دی، مننه. — زه موړ یم. — زه ډېر وږی یم.
بس دی، مننه — ډېر خوندور دی — هو، مننه — هو، ډېر موړ یم — حتماً راځم
ډېر خوندور دی. — زه موړ یم. — اوبه شته؟ — دا زمونږ دود دی. — زه ډېر وږی یم.
wave: If you eat with other people today, say ډېر خوندور دی to yourself before you take a bite. Praise that is never used evaporates; praise said every day will come out by itself when you are finally sitting on the floor of an Afghan home.
